16. Shallow Learning

CNRS & DMA, École Normale Supérieure

Chapter PDF · Complete book

Networks with one hidden layer provide a setting in which to ask which functions neural models can represent and how their size controls approximation error. These questions distinguish expressive power from the difficulty of fitting a model to data. We derive the training gradients, prove universal approximation, and develop quantitative bounds through Barron’s theorem, a representation by measures, and the Frank–Wolfe algorithm.

16.1 Multilayer Perceptrons¶

A multilayer perceptron (MLP) with one hidden layer has two trainable layers: a hidden layer and an output layer. Models with no hidden layer recover the linear predictors studied earlier. Deeper MLPs compose several layers; their derivatives are efficiently computed by the automatic differentiation methods of the multilayer-perceptron discussion.

16.1.1 Networks of Arbitrary Depth¶

We first define a network of arbitrary depth representing a map fθ:Rd→Rd′f_\theta : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^{d'}fθ​:Rd→Rd′.

Starting from x0=x∈Rd0=Rdx_0=x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_0}=\mathbb{R}^dx0​=x∈Rd0​=Rd, the network computes, for s=0,…,S−1s=0,\ldots,S-1s=0,…,S−1

xs+1=σ(Wsxs+bs)x_{s+1}=\sigma( W_s x_s + b_s )xs+1​=σ(Ws​xs​+bs​)

where Ws∈Rds+1×dsW_s \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{s+1} \times d_s}Ws​∈Rds+1​×ds​ and bs∈Rds+1b_s \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{s+1}}bs​∈Rds+1​. The output is fθ(x)=xSf_\theta(x)=x_Sfθ​(x)=xS​, with dS=d′d_S=d'dS​=d′ and parameters θ=((Ws,bs))s=0S−1\theta=((W_s,b_s))_{s=0}^{S-1}θ=((Ws​,bs​))s=0S−1​. The final activation can be omitted to obtain a linear output layer.

The activation σ\sigmaσ is a nonlinear, nonpolynomial function applied componentwise: σ(z)=(σ(zi))i\sigma(z) = (\sigma(z_i))_iσ(z)=(σ(zi​))i​.

Common activations include the sigmoid functions

σ(r)=er1+erandσ(r)=1πatan(r)+12\sigma(r) = \frac{e^r}{1+e^r} \quad \text{and} \quad \sigma(r) = \frac{1}{\pi} \text{atan}(r) + \frac{1}{2}σ(r)=1+erer​andσ(r)=π1​atan(r)+21​

and the rectified linear unit (ReLU), σ(r)=max⁡(r,0)\sigma(r)=\max(r,0)σ(r)=max(r,0). Sigmoids are bounded, whereas ReLU is unbounded and does not saturate on the positive half-line: its derivative is one there and zero on the negative half-line. The positive 1-homogeneity of ReLU allows weights to be rescaled, which is useful in proofs that restrict their directions to a unit sphere. At zero, ReLU is not differentiable. Implementations choose a derivative convention, while mathematical arguments must account for the kink.

For increasing width to yield universal approximation at fixed depth, the activation σ\sigmaσ must be nonpolynomial. Otherwise, fθf_\thetafθ​ has degree at most mSm^SmS for an activation of degree mmm and fixed depth SSS, so increasing the width cannot produce a dense class of continuous functions.

The choice σ=Id\sigma=\mathrm{Id}σ=Id remains useful for matrix factorization and supervised learning, but its input-output map is affine (linear when the biases vanish).

16.2 L∞L^\inftyL∞ Nonquantitative Universal Approximation¶

If σ\sigmaσ is a sigmoid function, George Cybenko’s theorem, later refined by Kurt Hornik, Maxwell Stinchcombe, and Halbert White, demonstrates that the functions fθf_\thetafθ​ can approximate any continuous function uniformly on a compact domain. Uniform approximation is stronger than the mean-square approximation used in the training loss (16.2).

Proposition 16.1

Let K⊂RdK \subset \mathbb{R}^dK⊂Rd be compact, and let σ\sigmaσ be nondecreasing, not necessarily continuous, with

lim⁡s→−∞σ(s)=0andlim⁡s→+∞σ(s)=1,\lim_{s \to -\infty} \sigma(s) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{s \to +\infty} \sigma(s) = 1,s→−∞lim​σ(s)=0ands→+∞lim​σ(s)=1,

Then, for any continuous function fff on KKK and any ε>0\varepsilon> 0ε>0, there exist nnn and parameters (θk)k=1n(\theta_k)_{k=1}^n(θk​)k=1n​ such that

sup⁡x∈K∣f(x)−fθ(x)∣⩽ε.\sup_{x \in K} |f(x) - f_\theta(x)| \leqslant\varepsilon.x∈Ksup​∣f(x)−fθ​(x)∣⩽ε.

The theorem establishes universal approximation by two-layer networks. It gives no quantitative bound on the number of neurons nnn needed for accuracy ε\varepsilonε, nor an efficient procedure for finding the parameters of fθf_\thetafθ​.

Cybenko [15] proved the result by duality. We present the more constructive argument of Hornik and collaborators, based on Stone–Weierstrass approximation by trigonometric functions. This density argument avoids relying on uniform convergence of Fourier partial sums, which need not hold for an arbitrary continuous function.

Proof

First establish density for networks with cosine activation; we will then approximate each cosine using the prescribed sigmoid σ\sigmaσ.

Consider the function space:

A:={∑k=1nukcos⁡(⟨vk,x⟩+bk):n∈N,(uk,bk,vk)k}.A := \left\{ \sum_{k=1}^n u_k \cos(\langle v_k, x \rangle + b_k) : n \in \mathbb{N}, (u_k, b_k, v_k)_k \right\}.A:={k=1∑n​uk​cos(⟨vk​,x⟩+bk​):n∈N,(uk​,bk​,vk​)k​}.

This space is an algebra: the product-to-sum identity expresses a product of cosines as a sum of two cosines. It contains constants and separates points. Indeed, for x≠x′x\neq x'x=x′, choose vvv so that ⟨v, x′−x⟩=π\langle v,\,x'-x\rangle=\pi⟨v,x′−x⟩=π and set b=−⟨v, x⟩b=-\langle v,\,x\rangleb=−⟨v,x⟩; the resulting cosine takes values 1 and -1 at these points. The Stone–Weierstrass theorem therefore implies that AAA is dense in C(K)C(K)C(K).

It remains to approximate each univariate cosine on a bounded interval by finite linear combinations of σ\sigmaσ. We give an argument that applies to any continuous function qqq on [a,b][a,b][a,b]. Choose a fine partition a=t0<⋯<tQ=ba=t_0<\cdots<t_Q=ba=t0​<⋯<tQ​=b and set Δj=q(tj)−q(tj−1)\Delta_j=q(t_j)-q(t_{j-1})Δj​=q(tj​)−q(tj−1​). Uniform continuity makes every ∣Δj∣|\Delta_j|∣Δj​∣ and the oscillation of qqq on each interval small. The staircase

q(t0)+∑j=1QΔj1[tj,+∞)(s)q(t_0)+\sum_{j=1}^Q\Delta_j1_{[t_j,+\infty)}(s)q(t0​)+j=1∑Q​Δj​1[tj​,+∞)​(s)

approximates qqq uniformly, up to this oscillation. Replace the step functions by σ(M(s−tj))\sigma(M(s-t_j))σ(M(s−tj​)). Choose disjoint small neighborhoods of the finitely many tjt_jtj​. Outside these neighborhoods, convergence to the steps is uniform as M→∞M\to\inftyM→∞; inside any one neighborhood, only one transition contributes a potentially large discrepancy, bounded by the small jump ∣Δj∣|\Delta_j|∣Δj​∣. Since 0⩽σ⩽10\leqslant\sigma\leqslant 10⩽σ⩽1, the resulting approximation is uniform. A constant is itself a neuron with zero inner weight and an appropriately scaled nonzero activation value.

Apply this construction to each cosine in a finite approximation of fff, choosing the individual errors small enough after weighting by the coefficients. Substitution of s=⟨vk, x⟩+bks=\langle v_k,\,x\rangle+b_ks=⟨vk​,x⟩+bk​ gives a finite network with uniform error at most ε\varepsilonε.

16.3 L2L^2L2 Quantitative Approximation (Barron’s Theorem)¶

We now study L2L^2L2 approximation, as measured by the loss (16.2). To isolate approximation error, assume noiseless observations y=f(x)y=f(x)y=f(x) for a target fff, with inputs xxx distributed according to ρ(x)\rho(x)ρ(x). We also assume that ρ\rhoρ is supported in a ball of radius RRR.

Without additional regularity, no uniform approximation rate follows: the error can decay arbitrarily slowly. Barron introduced a function class for which the approximation rate has an exponent independent of the ambient dimension.

16.3.1 Barron Space¶

For an integrable function fff, this section uses the following normalization of the Fourier transform at ξ∈Rd\xi \in \mathbb{R}^dξ∈Rd:

f^(ξ)≜(2π)−d∫Rdf(x)e−i⟨ξ, x⟩dx.\hat f(\xi)\triangleq(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}f(x)e^{-\mathrm{i}\langle \xi,\,x\rangle}\mathrm{d}x.f^​(ξ)≜(2π)−d∫Rd​f(x)e−i⟨ξ,x⟩dx.

The Barron space [1] is the class of functions for which the Fourier seminorm

∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣B≜∫Rd∣ ⁣∣ξ∣ ⁣∣∣f^(ξ)∣dξ|\!| f |\!|_B \triangleq \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}|\!| \xi |\!| | \hat{f}(\xi) | \mathrm{d}\xi∣∣f∣∣B​≜∫Rd​∣∣ξ∣∣∣f^​(ξ)∣dξ

is finite. Throughout this section, fff denotes its continuous Fourier-inversion representative, with the convention f(x)=∫f^(ξ)ei⟨ξ, x⟩dξf(x)=\int\hat f(\xi)e^{\mathrm{i}\langle \xi,\,x\rangle}\mathrm{d}\xif(x)=∫f^​(ξ)ei⟨ξ,x⟩dξ. For integrable fff, finiteness of the displayed seminorm ensures that f^\hat ff^​ is integrable: it is bounded near the origin, and its first moment controls the tail. This representative matters when the sampling measure has atoms. Constants can be handled separately; ∣f(0)∣+∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣B|f(0)|+|\!| f |\!|_B∣f(0)∣+∣∣f∣∣B​ removes the ambiguity due to constants in the corresponding Fourier-measure space. This Fourier-defined class should be distinguished from activation-dependent Barron spaces. One has

∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣B=∫Rd∣ ⁣∣∇f^(ξ)∣ ⁣∣dξ,|\!| f |\!|_B = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |\!| \widehat{\nabla f}(\xi) |\!| \mathrm{d}\xi,∣∣f∣∣B​=∫Rd​∣∣∇f​(ξ)∣∣dξ,

which relates the Fourier seminorm to first-order regularity.

The following examples illustrate the seminorm and its dependence on the function class.

  • Gaussians: for f(x)=e−∣ ⁣∣x∣ ⁣∣2/2f(x) = e^{- |\!| x |\!|^2/2}f(x)=e−∣∣x∣∣2/2, one has ∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣B=E∣ ⁣∣Z∣ ⁣∣⩽d,Z∼N(0,Idd)|\!| f |\!|_B=\mathbb{E}|\!| Z |\!|\leqslant\sqrt d,\quad Z\sim\mathcal N(0,\mathrm{Id}_d)∣∣f∣∣B​=E∣∣Z∣∣⩽d​,Z∼N(0,Idd​)

  • Ridge functions: for f(x)=ψ(⟨x, b⟩+c)f(x)=\psi(\langle x,\,b\rangle+c)f(x)=ψ(⟨x,b⟩+c), the Fourier transform may be a measure supported on a line rather than an integrable density. In the Fourier-measure extension of the seminorm,

    ∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣B⩽∣ ⁣∣b∣ ⁣∣∫R∣u∣ ∣ψ^(u)∣du.|\!| f |\!|_B\leqslant|\!| b |\!|\int_\mathbb{R}|u|\,|\hat\psi(u)|\mathrm{d}u.∣∣f∣∣B​⩽∣∣b∣∣∫R​∣u∣∣ψ^​(u)∣du.

    A sufficient condition is that ψ\psiψ is compactly supported and belongs to C2,δ(R)C^{2,\delta}(\mathbb{R})C2,δ(R) for some δ>0\delta>0δ>0. Smoothness alone without decay is not enough for this Fourier integral.

  • Sobolev functions: if s>d/2+1s>d/2+1s>d/2+1, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives

    ∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣B⩽C(d,s)∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣Hs,∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣Hs2:=∫Rd(1+∣ ⁣∣ξ∣ ⁣∣2)s∣f^(ξ)∣2dξ.|\!| f |\!|_B\leqslant C(d,s)|\!| f |\!|_{H^s},\qquad |\!| f |\!|_{H^s}^2\mathrel{:=}\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}(1+|\!| \xi |\!|^2)^s|\hat f(\xi)|^2\mathrm{d}\xi.∣∣f∣∣B​⩽C(d,s)∣∣f∣∣Hs​,∣∣f∣∣Hs2​:=∫Rd​(1+∣∣ξ∣∣2)s∣f^​(ξ)∣2dξ.

    Indeed, ∫∣ ⁣∣ξ∣ ⁣∣2(1+∣ ⁣∣ξ∣ ⁣∣2)−sdξ\int|\!| \xi |\!|^2(1+|\!| \xi |\!|^2)^{-s}\mathrm{d}\xi∫∣∣ξ∣∣2(1+∣∣ξ∣∣2)−sdξ is finite precisely when s>d/2+1s>d/2+1s>d/2+1. For integer sss, this squared Sobolev norm is equivalent, up to Fourier-normalization constants, to the sum of the squared L2L^2L2 norms of all weak derivatives of order at most sss. This is a sufficient condition; the Fourier-measure class also contains ridge functions outside these ambient-space Sobolev classes.

16.3.2 Barron’s Theorem¶

The main result is as follows.

Theorem 16.2 (Barron [1])

Assume ρ\rhoρ is a probability measure supported on B(0,R)B(0,R)B(0,R), fff is the continuous Fourier-inversion representative described above with ∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣B<∞|\!| f |\!|_B<\infty∣∣f∣∣B​<∞, and σ\sigmaσ is a nondecreasing sigmoid with limits 0 and 1. Allow an output bias c0c_0c0​, so the approximation is c0+fθc_0+f_\thetac0​+fθ​. For every n⩾1n\geqslant 1n⩾1,

inf⁡c0,θ∣ ⁣∣c0+fθ−f∣ ⁣∣L2(ρ)⩽2R∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣Bn.\inf_{c_0,\theta}|\!| c_0+f_\theta-f |\!|_{L^2(\rho)}\leqslant\frac{2R|\!| f |\!|_B}{\sqrt n}.c0​,θinf​∣∣c0​+fθ​−f∣∣L2(ρ)​⩽n​2R∣∣f∣∣B​​.

The infimum can be restricted to networks with ∑k=1n∣uk∣⩽2R∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣B\sum_{k=1}^n|u_k|\leqslant 2R|\!| f |\!|_B∑k=1n​∣uk​∣⩽2R∣∣f∣∣B​. In particular, for every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, a finite network attains the displayed bound plus ε\varepsilonε.

The exponent 1/21/21/2 in the approximation rate does not depend on the dimension. The constant ∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣B|\!| f |\!|_B∣∣f∣∣B​ can still depend on it: the Gaussian example gives growth of order d\sqrt dd​, whereas the bound for a fixed ridge profile depends on the ridge direction and profile.

16.3.3 Mean field representation.¶

Absorb a factor nnn into the outer coefficients uku_kuk​ to express the same network as an average:

fθ(x):=1n∑k=1nφ(x,ωk),f_\theta(x) := \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^n \varphi(x, \omega_k),fθ​(x):=n1​k=1∑n​φ(x,ωk​),

where θ=(ωk)k=1n\theta = (\omega_k)_{k=1}^nθ=(ωk​)k=1n​, ωk=(uk,vk,bk)∈Rd′×Rd+1\omega_k = (u_k, v_k, b_k) \in \mathbb{R}^{d'} \times \mathbb{R}^{d+1}ωk​=(uk​,vk​,bk​)∈Rd′×Rd+1 and φ(x,ω):=uσ(⟨v,x⟩+b)\varphi(x,\omega) := u \sigma(\langle v, x \rangle + b)φ(x,ω):=uσ(⟨v,x⟩+b). Introducing the empirical measure:

μ^:=1n∑k=1nδωk,\hat{\mu} := \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^n \delta_{\omega_k},μ^​:=n1​k=1∑n​δωk​​,

this neural network can be expressed as an integral:

fθ(x):=∫Ωφ(x,ω) dμ^(ω)f_\theta(x) := \int_\Omega \varphi(x, \omega) \, \mathrm{d}\hat{\mu}(\omega)fθ​(x):=∫Ω​φ(x,ω)dμ^​(ω)

where Ω⊂Rd′×Rd+1\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^{d'} \times \mathbb{R}^{d+1}Ω⊂Rd′×Rd+1 is the admissible parameter set. A uniform bound on uuu will be essential for the approximation estimate.

The representation is linear in the measure μ\muμ. It therefore extends naturally from empirical measures to general probability measures μ\muμ.

We now restrict to scalar outputs, d′=1d'=1d′=1.

The Fourier condition yields a bounded dictionary representation in a closure sense. This distinction matters: the assumptions do not automatically provide an exact probability measure on finite sigmoid parameters.

Proposition 16.3

Let M=2R∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣BM=2R|\!| f |\!|_BM=2R∣∣f∣∣B​. On K⊂B(0,R)K\subset B(0,R)K⊂B(0,R), the function f−f(0)f-f(0)f−f(0) belongs to the closed convex hull, in L2(ρ)L^2(\rho)L2(ρ), of the centered neurons

φω(x)=u(σ(⟨v, x⟩+b)−σ(b)),ω=(u,v,b),∣u∣⩽M.\varphi_\omega(x)=u\bigl(\sigma(\langle v,\,x\rangle+b)-\sigma(b)\bigr),\qquad \omega=(u,v,b),\quad |u|\leqslant M.φω​(x)=u(σ(⟨v,x⟩+b)−σ(b)),ω=(u,v,b),∣u∣⩽M.

Every dictionary element has L2(ρ)L^2(\rho)L2(ρ) norm at most MMM. For general measures μ\muμ on parameters, write

Φ(μ)(x)=∫φω(x)dμ(ω).(16.3)\Phi(\mu)(x)=\int\varphi_\omega(x)\mathrm{d}\mu(\omega). \tag{16.3}Φ(μ)(x)=∫φω​(x)dμ(ω).(16.3)

The proposition asserts membership in the closure of such averages, rather than existence of one exact average.

Proof sketch

Fourier inversion gives

f(x)−f(0)=∫(cos⁡(⟨ξ, x⟩+Θ(ξ))−cos⁡Θ(ξ))∣f^(ξ)∣dξ,f(x)-f(0)=\int\bigl(\cos(\langle \xi ,\,x\rangle+\Theta(\xi))-\cos\Theta(\xi)\bigr)|\hat f(\xi)|\mathrm{d}\xi,f(x)−f(0)=∫(cos(⟨ξ,x⟩+Θ(ξ))−cosΘ(ξ))∣f^​(ξ)∣dξ,

Step functions are limits of dilated sigmoids; choosing thresholds away from atoms of the projected data distribution, dominated convergence gives the same closed convex hull in L2(ρ)L^2(\rho)L2(ρ). A zero atom absorbs any unused coefficient mass. Centering the neurons accounts for an output bias when the sum is rewritten in the form (16.1).

For the next argument, write g=f−f(0)g=f-f(0)g=f−f(0). First suppose g=Φ(μ)g=\Phi(\mu)g=Φ(μ) exactly for a probability measure over this bounded dictionary. The same bound extends to ggg in its closed convex hull by approximating ggg arbitrarily closely before sampling.

16.3.5 Proof by optimization¶

A deterministic argument uses nnn Frank–Wolfe steps and its O(1/n)O(1/n)O(1/n) objective convergence rate.

For the centered target g=f−f(0)g=f-f(0)g=f−f(0), minimize over probability measures P(Ω)\mathcal{P}(\Omega)P(Ω):

inf⁡μ∈P(Ω)E(μ):=12∫K(Φ(μ)(x)−g(x))2 dρ(x),(16.4)\inf_{\mu \in \mathcal{P}(\Omega)} E(\mu) := \frac{1}{2} \int_K \left( \Phi(\mu)(x) - g(x) \right)^2 \, \mathrm{d}\rho(x), \tag{16.4}μ∈P(Ω)inf​E(μ):=21​∫K​(Φ(μ)(x)−g(x))2dρ(x),(16.4)

where ρ\rhoρ is the probability measure supported on KKK. This optimization problem is infinite-dimensional.

Ordinary network training instead restricts μ\muμ to an empirical measure and descends in the neuron parameters. This parameterization is nonconvex. Chizat and Bach relate suitable mean-field limits to Wasserstein gradient flows and prove global convergence under additional structural and initialization assumptions. Such results do not imply that every sufficiently wide finite network, initialized from an arbitrary density, avoids all nonglobal stationary points.

The deterministic approximation argument below uses convex optimization over measures. Its linear minimization oracle is a global optimization problem over a single neuron’s parameters and may itself be computationally difficult in high dimensions. Since the parameter domain need not be compact, exact oracle minimizers may fail to exist; approximate oracles or closure arguments then replace exact minimization.

First order variations.

We derive the algorithm by linearizing the objective on measures equipped with the total variation norm. The same construction applies to differentiable convex objectives on a Banach space.

We write integration as a pairing between a function and a measure:

⟨f, μ⟩:=∫f(x)dμ(x).\langle f,\,\mu\rangle := \int f(x) \mathrm{d} \mu(x).⟨f,μ⟩:=∫f(x)dμ(x).

Let μ+εη\mu+\varepsilon\etaμ+εη be a small perturbation of μ\muμ, where η\etaη is a finite signed measure.

The first variation ∇E(μ)\nabla E(\mu)∇E(μ) represents the derivative through the expansion

E(μ+εη)=E(μ)+ε⟨∇E(μ), η⟩+o(ε),E(\mu+\varepsilon\eta) = E(\mu) + \varepsilon\langle \nabla E(\mu),\,\eta\rangle + o(\varepsilon),E(μ+εη)=E(μ)+ε⟨∇E(μ),η⟩+o(ε),

Thus ∇E(μ)\nabla E(\mu)∇E(μ) represents the Fréchet derivative of EEE. For the present quadratic objective,

E(μ+εη)=12∫K(Φ(μ)(x)−g(x)+εΦ(η)(x))2 dρ(x),E(\mu+\varepsilon\eta) = \frac{1}{2} \int_K \left( \Phi(\mu)(x) - g(x) + \varepsilon\Phi(\eta)(x) \right)^2 \, \mathrm{d}\rho(x),E(μ+εη)=21​∫K​(Φ(μ)(x)−g(x)+εΦ(η)(x))2dρ(x),

which expands to:

E(μ+εη)=E(μ)+ε∫KΦ(η)(x)(Φ(μ)(x)−g(x)) dρ(x)+O(ε2).E(\mu+\varepsilon\eta) = E(\mu) + \varepsilon\int_K \Phi(\eta)(x) \left( \Phi(\mu)(x) - g(x) \right) \, \mathrm{d}\rho(x) + O(\varepsilon^2).E(μ+εη)=E(μ)+ε∫K​Φ(η)(x)(Φ(μ)(x)−g(x))dρ(x)+O(ε2).

Rewriting this in terms of φ\varphiφ, we find:

∇E(μ)(ω)=∫Kφ(x,ω)(Φ(μ)(x)−g(x)) dρ(x).\nabla E(\mu)(\omega) = \int_K \varphi(x, \omega) \left( \Phi(\mu)(x) - g(x) \right) \, \mathrm{d}\rho(x).∇E(μ)(ω)=∫K​φ(x,ω)(Φ(μ)(x)−g(x))dρ(x).

It is a bounded function of ω\omegaω; continuity follows when the activation and parameterization are continuous.

Frank-Wolfe algorithm.

Frank–Wolfe minimizes a differentiable convex function over a convex subset of a Banach space:

min⁡μ∈CE(μ).\min_{\mu \in \mathcal{C}} E(\mu).μ∈Cmin​E(μ).

Each step linearizes the objective E(μ)E(\mu)E(μ).

Choose an initial measure μ0\mu_0μ0​, for example a Dirac mass. At iteration kkk, update with step size τk\tau_kτk​:

μk+1=(1−τk)μk+τkνk∗,\mu_{k+1} = (1 - \tau_k) \mu_k + \tau_k \nu_k^*,μk+1​=(1−τk​)μk​+τk​νk∗​,

where νk∗\nu_k^*νk∗​ minimizes the linearized objective:

νk∗∈arg⁡min⁡ν∈P(Ω)⟨∇E(μk), ν⟩\nu_k^* \in \arg\min_{\nu \in \mathcal{P}(\Omega)} \langle \nabla E(\mu_k),\,\nu\rangleνk∗​∈argν∈P(Ω)min​⟨∇E(μk​),ν⟩

This linear minimization step is called an oracle. On a finite parameter grid it amounts to comparing finitely many values. Over a continuous neuron parameter space Ω\OmegaΩ, it is generally a nonconvex optimization problem.

Here C=P(Ω)\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{P}(\Omega)C=P(Ω) carries the total variation norm ∥μ∥TV=∣μ∣(Ω)\|\mu\|_{\mathrm{TV}} = |\mu|(\Omega)∥μ∥TV​=∣μ∣(Ω), the measure analogue of the L1L^1L1 norm.

In this special case, a key property of the algorithm is that the solution νk∗\nu_k^*νk∗​ can be taken as a Dirac measure when the minimum over Ω\OmegaΩ is attained since, denoting gk:=∇E(μk)g_k := \nabla E(\mu_k)gk​:=∇E(μk​),

νk∗=δωk∗,where ωk∗∈arg⁡min⁡ω∈Ωgk(ω).\nu_k^* = \delta_{\omega_k^*}, \quad \text{where } \omega_k^* \in \arg\min_{\omega \in \Omega} g_k(\omega).νk∗​=δωk∗​​,where ωk∗​∈argω∈Ωmin​gk​(ω).

This holds because for any ν∈P(Ω)\nu \in \mathcal{P}(\Omega)ν∈P(Ω):

∫gk(ω) dν(ω)⩾min⁡(gk),\int g_k(\omega) \, \mathrm{d}\nu(\omega) \geqslant\min(g_k),∫gk​(ω)dν(ω)⩾min(gk​),

and equality is achieved when ν=δωk∗\nu = \delta_{\omega_k^*}ν=δωk∗​​. Therefore, if μ0\mu_0μ0​ is initialized as a Dirac measure, each iteration of the algorithm ensures that μk\mu_kμk​ remains a sum of at most k+1k+1k+1 Dirac masses.

Convergence Rate

The next theorem gives the Frank–Wolfe convergence rate.

In our case, ∥⋅∥=∥⋅∥TV\|\cdot\|=\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{TV}}∥⋅∥=∥⋅∥TV​ is the total variation norm of measures. Bounded functions paired with these measures carry the supremum norm ∥⋅∥∞\|\cdot\|_{\infty}∥⋅∥∞​. Throughout this argument, L∞L^\inftyL∞ denotes the pointwise supremum norm, so values at atoms are retained.

We first establish the quadratic upper bound implied by a Lipschitz gradient.

Lemma 16.4

Let C\mathcal CC be convex, and let E:C→RE: \mathcal{C} \to \mathbb{R}E:C→R be differentiable with LLL-Lipschitz gradient with respect to the norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\|∥⋅∥. That is, for all μ,ν∈C\mu, \nu \in \mathcal{C}μ,ν∈C,

∥∇E(μ)−∇E(ν)∥∗⩽L∥ν−μ∥,\|\nabla E(\mu) - \nabla E(\nu)\|_* \leqslant L \|\nu - \mu\|,∥∇E(μ)−∇E(ν)∥∗​⩽L∥ν−μ∥,

For the objective EEE in (16.4), the proposition below gives L⩽M2L\leqslant M^2L⩽M2 with M=2R∥f∥BM=2R\|f\|_BM=2R∥f∥B​. The total variation diameter of probability measures is D=2D=2D=2, and ∥f∥B\|f\|_B∥f∥B​ denotes the Barron seminorm of the target fff.

When the linear oracle attains its minimum, Frank–Wolfe constructs a measure μk\mu_kμk​ supported on at most k+1k+1k+1 points, with objective error
